title: How to add subtitles to a YouTube video in Studio on Mac, step by step

description: Add subtitles in YouTube Studio on your Mac: upload a caption file, auto-sync a transcript, or type the lines. Costs, fixes, and a five-day plan.

intro: To add subtitles to a YouTube video in Studio, open YouTube Studio in Chrome, click Subtitles in the left menu, choose the video, and click ADD LANGUAGE. Under Subtitles, click ADD, then pick Upload file, Auto-sync, or Type manually. Before you start, you need a caption file or a transcript. A caption file must be plain UTF-8 text.
tldr: Menu path: YouTube Studio > Subtitles > your video > ADD LANGUAGE > ADD under Subtitles.
Pick Upload file for a caption file, Auto-sync for a transcript, or Type manually for short videos.
Save SRT or SBV files as plain UTF-8. YouTube does not recognize styling markup in them.
Skip auto-sync for videos over an hour or with poor audio. YouTube's help page advises against it.
Read automatic captions before you publish. Accuracy claims conflict, so test your own video.

blocks.text: Add subtitles in YouTube Studio, step by step

Start in Chrome, because YouTube Studio runs in your browser. Sign in with the Google account that owns the channel. Open the video you want to caption. The steps below follow YouTube's help page, so the menu names match what you see on screen.

items: Click Subtitles in the left menu of YouTube Studio.
Choose your video from the list.
Click ADD LANGUAGE and choose the language of the spoken words.
Pick Upload file, Auto-sync, or Type manually.
Save, then play the video with captions on and check the timing.

blocks.text: The short menu path is YouTube Studio > Subtitles > your video > ADD LANGUAGE > ADD. Write it in your notes once. Each step is one click, so you can stop at any point and come back to it later.
Upload, auto-sync, or type: which option fits

Each option asks for something different. Upload file takes a caption file you already made. Auto-sync takes a transcript you type or paste, and YouTube lines it up with the audio. Type manually takes the words one line at a time, and YouTube sets the timing for you.

rows: An SRT, SBV, WebVTT, or TTML file
SRT and SBV get basic support only, and styling is ignored
A full transcript, typed or pasted
Not recommended for videos over an hour or with poor audio
Slow for longer videos, since you type every line
blocks.caption: The three subtitle options in YouTube Studio compared

blocks.text: If you already have a caption file, upload it. If you only have a script, auto-sync is the faster route. Type manually suits a short video when you want full control of every word.
Auto-sync: how to get a transcript to line up

Auto-sync needs your words to match the recording. Paste the transcript as it was spoken, including repeats and false starts. Remove stage notes such as [music] unless you want them in the captions. A transcript that drifts from the audio puts lines in the wrong places.

YouTube's help page says auto-sync is not recommended for videos over an hour long, or for poor audio quality. For those videos, skip auto-sync. Upload a caption file that you read through yourself. It takes longer, but you know what viewers will see.
What YouTube's automatic captions cover and how accurate they are

Studio can also create automatic captions with speech recognition. YouTube's help page says these run only in the video's default language. For a second language, you add it yourself with ADD LANGUAGE.

Accuracy is the harder question, and the sources disagree. Panopto says speech recognition captions are typically 90 to 95% accurate, depending on audio quality. 3Play Media says YouTube's free automatic captions run 60 to 70% accurate. Neither figure tests your video, so check your own.

blocks.title: Do not publish unchecked captions
blocks.text: Automatic captions can miss names, brand terms, and numbers. One wrong word in a claim can change what viewers think you said. Read every caption that carries a fact before you publish.
Why captions are worth the time you put in

Captions do more than help deaf and hard-of-hearing viewers. Gernsbacher's 2015 review says more than 100 empirical studies link captions to better comprehension, attention, and memory. The strongest benefits, the review says, show up for non-native speakers and people learning to read.

Viewers use subtitles a lot. The XR Global Accessibility Report, released in May 2026, surveyed 3,000 consumers in five countries. It found 79% of UK viewers use subtitles at least sometimes. Among 18 to 24 year olds, 59% use them always or often.
What adding subtitles really costs
Most of the cost is time. Sources give few clean numbers for creators, so the figures here come from vendors. Treat them as estimates, and time one of your own videos before you plan a batch.

3Play Media's per-minute range works out to $60 to $900 for one hour of video. That is arithmetic on a vendor's quoted range, not a price for your project. Panopto says human captions typically arrive in two to five days.
Mac apps that make caption files for YouTube

Final Cut Pro is the Mac option with built-in caption generation. Apple's guide for version 12.4 says Generate Captions needs a Mac with Apple silicon. It works in U.S. English only. Choose Edit > Generate Captions > Subtitles, or press Shift-Command-S.

iMovie is a common dead end. Apple's iMovie for Mac user guide does not mention captions, subtitles, SRT import, or speech to text. Its title tools are the only on-screen text it covers. Do not plan your captions around iMovie.

MacWhisper is a Mac transcription app that exports .srt and .vtt files, according to its website. The site lists a free plan and a Pro plan at €64 per license with lifetime updates. It does not say which plan includes subtitle export, so check before you pay.

Descript's free plan is $0. It includes 60 media minutes per month, 720p export, and a watermark. The paid Hobbyist plan lists 600 minutes per month, 1080p, and no watermark. Dynamic captions are listed as unlimited on all four self-serve plans.
Mistakes that cost you a second pass

items: Uploading a file with styling markup. YouTube does not recognize styling in SRT or SBV files.
Using auto-sync on a video over an hour, or on noisy audio.
Skipping ADD LANGUAGE, so a second language never gets added.
Editing the video after captioning, so the timing no longer matches the cut.
Saving the caption file as rich text instead of plain UTF-8.
Pasting dictated text into auto-sync without checking it against the recording.

blocks.text: Where Lazur helps, and where it does not

Lazur does not add captions to your video. It does not click buttons, edit files, or run other apps for you. It points, guides, and explains. That covers the parts of this job that slow people down: finding the right menu, reading a file error, and checking what a term means.

Hold ⌥ ⌘ and ask where Subtitles sits in YouTube Studio. Lazur draws a circle and a label around it on your screen and answers out loud. To upload, ask Lazur to walk you through it. It guides you one click at a time, waiting for each click before it moves on.

Dictation is a separate feature. Hold fn to dictate clean, formatted text at the cursor in any app. You can speak a script into Google Docs and paste it into auto-sync later. Check the result against your recording first, because clean text can differ from what you say.
For a wider search, such as which caption tools export .srt files, Lazur can run research in its own Chrome tabs. It returns a summary and a report. You still decide which tool fits your videos.
Privacy and client footage
Lazur listens and looks at your screen only while you hold the shortcut. Audio and the screenshot go to AI providers to answer you, and they are not stored. Content is never used to train AI models.

If the footage or transcript includes client or patient material, follow your employer's rules on that data before you upload it. That applies to any caption or transcription tool, including YouTube, Descript, MacWhisper, and Lazur.
Next step: pick one video and check it

Pick one video that already has a transcript or script. Work through the steps above, then play it with captions on and sound off. If the words make sense without audio, the file is ready. Repeat the routine for the next video.

faq.question: Can I add subtitles to a YouTube video in Studio without a file?
faq.answer: Yes. Open Subtitles in YouTube Studio, choose the video, click ADD LANGUAGE, then ADD under Subtitles. Pick Type manually or Auto-sync, and type or paste your words. For short clips, type manually.

faq.question: Does YouTube add subtitles on its own?
faq.answer: Studio can create automatic captions with speech recognition. They run only in the video's default language. Accuracy depends on audio quality, and sources disagree on how accurate they are, so read them before you publish.

faq.question: Which subtitle file format should I upload?
faq.answer: Use SRT or SBV if that is what your tool exports, and save the text as plain UTF-8. YouTube supports those two only at a basic level. WebVTT and TTML support positioning and styling, if you need that.

faq.question: Why did my auto-sync fail?
faq.answer: The usual causes are a video over an hour, poor audio, and a transcript that does not match the recording. Check those first. Then try again with a transcript that matches the spoken words.

faq.question: Can I add subtitles in iMovie on a Mac?
faq.answer: Apple's iMovie for Mac user guide does not mention captions, subtitles, SRT import, or speech to text. Titles are the only on-screen text it covers. For caption generation on a Mac, Apple documents Final Cut Pro instead.

faq.question: Do I need Final Cut Pro to caption a video?
faq.answer: No. You can caption directly in YouTube Studio. Final Cut Pro helps if you edit there and want subtitle clips made from speech. Apple's guide says it needs Apple silicon and works in U.S. English only.

faq.question: Is there a free way to make a caption file?
faq.answer: Yes, with limits. Descript's free plan includes 60 media minutes per month. MacWhisper lists a free plan, but its site does not say which plan includes subtitle export. Check that before you rely on it.

faq.question: Can Lazur add the subtitles for me?
faq.answer: No. Lazur does not click buttons or edit files for you. It can point at the Subtitles menu, guide you one click at a time, explain a file format, and dictate text at the cursor.

faq.question: Do I have to follow rules for client footage?
faq.answer: If the video or transcript holds client or patient material, follow your employer's rules on that data before you upload it. That applies to any caption or transcription tool, including YouTube and Lazur.

costs.title: Your time to make the transcript
costs.text: A transcript is the slow part. Auto-sync still needs the words, and someone has to type or paste them. Panopto says its automatic captions take about one-quarter of video length, which is about 15 minutes for an hour of video. That is a vendor estimate, so time one of your own videos first.

costs.title: A second pass after a bad upload
costs.text: A caption file that fails on upload, or a transcript that drifts, costs you another round. Each round means another edit, another upload, and another check with sound on and off. Plan for at least one correction pass on every video. Skipping that pass means viewers see the mistakes.

costs.title: Paid human captions
costs.text: 3Play Media says professional captioning runs $1 to $15 per minute. For one hour of video, that range works out to $60 to $900. Panopto says human captions are typically delivered in two to five days, so plan lead time. Get a quote from the provider before you commit.

costs.title: Tool subscriptions
costs.text: Descript's free plan is $0 and includes 60 media minutes per month. Its paid Hobbyist plan lists 600 minutes per month. MacWhisper lists a free plan and a Pro plan at €64 per license. Check each provider's pricing page for current terms before you choose.

costs.title: The reach you lose without captions
costs.text: The cost of skipping captions is harder to see. Gernsbacher's review links captions to better comprehension, attention, and memory. The XR report found 79% of UK viewers use subtitles at least sometimes. A video without them asks more of viewers who need or prefer them.

causes.title: The transcript and the audio do not match
causes.text: Auto-sync is a matching job. If the words you paste differ from the audio, the lines fall in the wrong places. Scripts change in the edit, and a line you cut can still sit in the transcript. Re-check the transcript after every edit, not only at the start.

causes.title: Auto-sync limits on long or noisy audio
causes.text: YouTube's help page says auto-sync is not recommended for videos over an hour long, or for poor audio quality. A long recording with a fan, an echo, or several voices makes matching harder. Those videos need a caption file you checked yourself, not a quick paste.

causes.title: Caption file formats YouTube reads only partly
causes.text: YouTube supports SRT and SBV only at a basic level. Styling markup is not recognized, and files must be plain UTF-8. WebVTT and TTML support positioning and styling. Many editors export styled files by default, so the file you upload may carry markup YouTube ignores.

causes.title: Automatic captions cover one language
causes.text: Studio creates automatic captions in the video's default language only. If part of your audience reads another language, that version is manual work. Each language gets its own entry under ADD LANGUAGE, so each one needs its own pass and its own check.

causes.title: Speech recognition accuracy varies
causes.text: Panopto says accuracy depends on audio quality. The sources give different ranges for YouTube's own automatic captions. A weak microphone, strong accents, and jargon all push accuracy down. Names, brands, and technical terms are the words to check first.

causes.title: Picking a Mac tool that cannot make captions
causes.text: Apple's iMovie guide does not document captions. Final Cut Pro's caption generation needs Apple silicon and works in U.S. English only. If you pick the wrong app, you lose time before you reach Studio. Check the tool's documentation for caption export, not only for text or titles.

causes.title: Extra work falls on creators
causes.text: A 2022 study by Li and colleagues looked at how individual creators caption. It interviewed 13 DHH viewers, analyzed 189 captioning-related videos, and surveyed 62 creators. A separate paper by Vogler and colleagues describes a deaf content creation tax, the extra time Deaf creators need to match peers. Captioning is often that extra time.

fixes.title: Upload a file you checked yourself
fixes.text: Build the caption file in your own tool, read it through, then upload it under ADD > Upload file. The timing comes from your file, so auto-sync's matching step is skipped. You also control the wording, line by line.

fixes.title: Make a plain UTF-8 SRT file on your Mac
fixes.text: Open TextEdit. If the window shows rich text, choose Format > Make Plain Text. Type or paste your lines in SRT form. Each block has a number, a timestamp line with an arrow, the caption text, and a blank line. TextEdit can add .txt when you save, so check that the name ends in .srt.

fixes.title: Split long videos before you caption them
fixes.text: YouTube does not recommend auto-sync for videos over an hour. For a long video, skip auto-sync and upload a file you read through. Reading takes longer, but the result is predictable, and the timing stays with your file.

fixes.title: Check automatic captions in three places
fixes.text: Automatic captions are a draft. Play the opening minute, a middle section, and the closing minute with captions on. Mark every wrong name, number, or term. Fix the source transcript, then upload a corrected file. Sources disagree on accuracy, so a sample check is the fairest test for your video.

fixes.title: Give each language its own pass
fixes.text: Automatic captions cover the default language only. For a second language, go to Subtitles, click ADD LANGUAGE, then add the file or transcript for that language. Check each one separately. A mistake in one language stays there until you fix it.

fixes.title: Confirm the export before you rely on it
fixes.text: In Final Cut Pro, Generate Captions works on Apple silicon in U.S. English. The output is subtitle title clips on the timeline. Check that your export step can write a caption file YouTube reads. This page does not cover that export, so confirm it in your version of the app.

fixes.title: Trial a free tool on one short video
fixes.text: Descript's free plan includes 60 media minutes per month and 100 one-time AI credits. MacWhisper has a free plan. Run one short video through a free option first. Confirm subtitle export on MacWhisper's website before you build a workflow around it.

fixes.title: Run a sound-off check before you publish
fixes.text: Play the video with sound off and captions on. If the words make sense without audio, the captions are doing their job. If you have to rewind to follow, the timing or wording needs work. Fix the file, upload it again, and repeat the check.

plan.label: Day 1
plan.title: List the videos that need captions
plan.text: Make a short list of videos without captions. Mark each one as having a script, a transcript, or nothing yet. Start with the ones that already have a transcript, since they take the least work.

plan.label: Day 2
plan.title: Check what Studio already has
plan.text: Open YouTube Studio in Chrome and click Subtitles in the left menu. Look at each video's language list. Note which languages are already added and which are missing.

plan.label: Day 3
plan.title: Build one caption file you can trust
plan.text: Take one transcript and make an SRT file in a plain text editor. Save it with the .srt ending. Read every line once with the video open beside it. Fix names and numbers first.

plan.label: Day 4
plan.title: Upload, play, and check
plan.text: Click ADD LANGUAGE, then ADD under Subtitles, and choose Upload file. Play the video with captions on. Fix any line that appears too early or too late, then upload the corrected file.

plan.label: Day 5
plan.title: Handle the harder cases
plan.text: Use Type manually for short videos. Skip auto-sync for anything over an hour or with poor audio. Add a second language only after the first one is correct.

plan.label: Ongoing
plan.title: Make captions part of publishing
plan.text: Add a line to your publishing checklist: captions checked before the video goes public. Keep one plain UTF-8 caption file per language in the same folder as the video file.
